newsitem.title: USA: Clinton says U.S. must ratify chemical treaty.
newsitem.headline: Clinton says U.S. must ratify chemical treaty.

text.p: President Bill Clinton said on Tuesday in response to conservative Republican criticism that the United States must ratify a treaty banning chemical weapons to avoid being seen as a rogue state.

"I think it's critically important for America," he told reporters as North Carolina Sen. Jesse Helms, a conservative Republican, held hearings on the treaty in the Senate Foreign Relations Committee that he chairs.
Helms was hearing from opponents including former defence secretaries Casper Weinberger, James Schlesinger and Donald Rumsfeld. Later he was to hear from Secretary of State Madeleine Albright.
Clinton said he wanted to get the treaty out of Helms' committee to the floor of the Senate and seek a two-thirds vote from the 100-member Senate.

"If we don't ratify it then the rest of the world will be compelled to treat us like rogue states, to basically ostracize us and impose trade sanctions on our chemical companies, and we'll deserve it if we don't ratify it because we won't be good citizens in the world," he said.
He said he had been working hard to answer Helms' objections. "We've got to get it out of the committee and then we've got to have 67 votes," he said.
Last week Clinton held a rally at the White House for the Chemical Weapons Convention, bringing in ex-Secretary of State James Baker, a Republican, to press his case.

The treaty was signed by the United States and 129 other countries in Paris on January 12, 1993. Although at last count 161 countries had signed and about 70 ratified the treaty, it has languished in the U.S. Senate since 1993.
If the Senate fails to approve it by April 29, the United States will lose the right to be regarded as a charter signatory, which backers say would severely restrict the U.S. role in enforcing it.
